Eat the way you run

Eating well to run well is simpler than you think. Here are the essentials, no jargon: daily, before a race, during, after.

Daily fueling

Eating well to run is the basics done right: enough pasta, rice and bread for energy, meat/fish/eggs/legumes to repair muscles, water all day. No magic. Just consistency.

Carbs

5-7 g/kg

Your weight × 5 to 7. Ex: 70 kg → 350-490 g/day of pasta, rice, bread

Protein

1.8 g/kg

Ex: 70 kg → 126 g/day. A portion of meat/fish = 25-30 g

Fat

1 g/kg

Olive oil, avocado, nuts, oily fish first

Water

30-35 ml/kg

Ex: 70 kg → 2 to 2.5 L/day. Add 500 ml per running hour

The 1:0.8 ratio — the new carb rule

For long efforts, your body absorbs two types of sugar better together than one alone. That's how pros eat up to 120 g of sugar per hour without stomach trouble. The right mix: a bit more glucose than fructose, in a 1 to 0.8 ratio. Maurten, Precision Fuel, SiS Beta Fuel all use this principle.

Glucose alone

1:0

60 g/h max — you hit the ceiling fast

Mix 2:1

2:1

90 g/h — the old reference

Best

Mix 1:0.8

1:0.8

120 g/h — top range for pros

Homemade recipe: 50 g maltodextrin + 40 g fructose + a pinch of salt in 500 ml water. The salt isn't trivial: it actually helps your body absorb sugar faster.

Protein: 1.8 g/kg, in 4 doses

The old recommendations (1.2 to 1.6 g/kg) are outdated. Runners need more protein than we used to think: about 1.8 g per kilo of body weight. Even more important: spread it across 4 meals during the day rather than 1 or 2 big ones. Your muscles repair better that way.

For 5 to 7 days after a 50 km+ race

  1. Breakfast

    30 g

    Eggs, cottage cheese, skyr — not just bread and jam

  2. Lunch

    Cottage cheese works fine. Feeds your muscles all night

To repair muscles properly, you need at least 25-30 g of complete protein per meal (meat, fish, eggs, cottage cheese, mix of legumes+grains). Below that, the effect is weak. Above, it plateaus.

Coffee before a race

Coffee (or caffeine) is one of the few products that really works to run better. Count 3 to 6 mg per kilo of your weight, taken 60 minutes before the start. For 70 kg, that's 210 to 420 mg, or 2 to 4 cups. In capsule form, the dosing is more precise. One thing to know: some people metabolize coffee slowly (genetics). They feel the opposite — palpitations, stomach aches. If that's you, drop to 1-2 mg/kg or skip it.

  1. T-90 min

    Coffee or capsule. If you don't drink it daily: 3 mg/kg. If you do: 6 mg/kg.

  2. T-60 min

    Caffeine peaks in your blood now. Use this time to finish hydrating and hit the bathroom.

  3. T-30 min

    You start warming up. No more coffee now — it would kick in too late.

  4. Race start

    Full effect for 3-4 hours. On an ultra, you can take a small dose again mid-race.

When to be careful

  • No coffee after 2 PM if you race early next day. Your body takes 5 hours to remove half of it.
  • If you feel palpitations, anxiety or stomach aches: it's too much for you. Cut down or stop.
  • Combined with a long effort, coffee can speed up your gut (urgent need). Test in training, not race day.
  • Golden rule: never try a new dose on race day. Always test 2 to 3 times before.
  • If coffee makes you nervous even at small doses, you might be among slow metabolizers. Try 1 or 2 mg/kg, or skip.

Hydration: drink when you're thirsty

For a long time, the rule was "drink before you're thirsty." That's wrong, and even dangerous. Science since 2015 says the opposite: thirst is a good signal, trust it. Drinking too much has become riskier than drinking too little (a runner died at the Boston Marathon in 2002 from over-drinking). Simple trick: the color of your urine in the morning tells you everything. Pale yellow = good. Dark = drink more. Clear = drink less.

On waking

400-500 ml

A big glass of plain water after 8 hours of fasting

Throughout the day

1.5 to 2 L

Steady small sips, not big gulps

Evening

200-300 ml

Stop 1 hour before bed to avoid waking up at night

During the run: 500 to 800 ml per hour depending on how much you sweat. Beyond 1 hour of effort, add salt (0.5-0.7 g per liter, about a small pinch). On an ultra, up to 1 g of salt per hour. Never go over 800 ml of plain water per hour: risk of water intoxication (rare but serious). No ibuprofen or anti-inflammatories during a race: they block kidney water elimination.

The week before the race

The goal of this week: fill your muscles with energy (glycogen) without tiring them. The 80s method (3 days of starvation then 3 days of loading) is outdated. Today: drop training volume, gradually raise pasta/rice/bread, and sleep. You'll gain 1 to 2 kg on the scale these last days: that's normal. Each gram of stored energy holds 3 grams of water.

  1. D-7

    Cut volume

    Volume divided by 5. Keep short intensity. Regular balanced meals.

    Step 1 of 8
  2. D-6

    Cut excesses

    No alcohol (it harms muscle repair). No fried foods or heavy meals.

    Step 2 of 8
  3. D-5

    More carbs

    Pasta, rice, sweet potato, bread. Aim 6 to 8 g of carbs per kilo of weight.

    Step 3 of 8
  4. D-4

    Hydrate well

    1.5 to 2 L of water + a drink with a bit of salt. Pale-yellow urine.

    Step 4 of 8
  5. D-3

    Carb load

    Now 10 to 12 g of carbs per kilo (so 700-800 g for 70 kg). Prefer simple sources: white pasta, white rice, white bread.

    Step 5 of 8
  6. D-2

    Shake-out run

    20-30 min easy to stay sharp without tiring. Nothing new: no new gel, no new shoes, no never-worn clothes. Whatever you'll use on race day must have been broken in over weeks.

    Step 6 of 8
  7. D-1

    Meal and prep

    Familiar dinner, carb-rich and low-fiber (no big raw vegetables). Bed early. Lay out bib, clothes, gels, shoes, watch — everything ready the night before to save time in the morning.

    Step 7 of 8
  8. Race day

    Breakfast 3 h before

    1 to 3 g of carbs per kilo, easy to digest. 500 ml of water. Last coffee 90 min before the start.

    Step 8 of 8

Before the effort

The closer you get to the start, the more you want quick sugar in small amounts. Your stomach should be quiet at the start. Golden rule: nothing new on race day. What you eat that day, you've already tested on long runs, several times.

T-3 h

1 to 3 g/kg of carbs

Familiar meal, low fiber and fat. Ex: white pasta + chicken breast + ripe banana

T-1 h

30 to 60 g of carbs

Light snack: ripe banana, applesauce, white bread with honey

T-15 min

Gel or drink

Optional. Useful mainly if the race lasts more than 1 h 30

During the effort

Beyond 1 hour of effort, eating really makes a difference. Aim for 60 to 90 g of sugar per hour (1 gel = 25 g on average). Elite runners go up to 120 g/h, but that takes weeks of digestive training. The trap: don't wait until you're hungry or thirsty. Start at minute 30, in small regular amounts.

DistanceSugar per hourRecommended mixTypical total
5 km (under 30 min)0-30 g/h—Plain water is enough
10 km (40-60 min)30-60 g/h1:01 to 2 gels or 500 ml of drink
Half (~1 h 30)60-90 g/h2:12 to 3 gels + drink
Marathon (3-4 h)90 g/h1:0.85 to 7 gels + sports drink
Elite (under 3 h)120 g/h1:0.8120 g/h, trained stomach
Ultra (over 4 h)60-90 g/h1:0.8Mix of solids + gels + drink + salty soup

Train your stomach — 6 to 12 week protocol

  1. 1

    Wk 1-2

    30 g/h

    Start gentle, on runs over 1 h 30.

  2. 2

    Wk 3-4

    60 g/h

    The stomach gradually adapts.

  3. 3

    Wk 5-6

    90 g/h

    You hit the standard target.

  4. 4

    Wk 7+

    120 g/h

    Pro level. 1:0.8 mix mandatory.

After the effort

We long believed you had to eat in the 30 minutes after exercise. False: the real window is wider. Your body keeps absorbing for 4 to 6 hours for sugars, and 24 to 48 h for proteins. If you go home and eat normally within 2 hours, you're fine. The short window only really matters if you have a 2nd session that same day.

0 to 30 min

Quick refill

If you have another session in less than 4 h: 1 to 1.2 g of sugar + 0.3 g of protein per kilo. Chocolate milk works great (proven by science). Otherwise, the next meal is enough.

0 to 2 h

Full meal

Carbs + protein + a little fat + vegetables. Drink up to 1.5× what you lost sweating. Tart cherry and turmeric help recovery (2024 scientific evidence).

24 to 48 h

Deep repair

Spread protein across 4 doses of 25-30 g. 40 g of cottage cheese before sleep. Sleep long. Avoid alcohol: it cuts muscle repair by 24%.

Supplements — what actually works

The Australian Institute of Sport classified all popular supplements in 4 levels based on scientific evidence. Out of 28 common products with runners, only 5 have solid proof. Others range from "interesting in some cases" to "pure marketing claim." Here are the 17 you should know.

AWorks

Caffeine

The most proven supplement for running. Improves performance by 2 to 7% on long efforts. In capsule form, dosing is precise.

Dose

3-6 mg/kg

When

60 min before

AWorks

Creatine

Drop the myth: it doesn't bulk you up like a bodybuilder. The +1 kg is water held in the muscles. Useful for ultras, trail, after 40, and during double-session blocks.

Dose

3-5 g/day

When

Year-round

AWorks

Bicarbonate

Helps neutralize muscle acidity on short, intense efforts. Maurten Bicarb System avoids stomach issues. Useless beyond marathon.

Dose

0.2-0.3 g/kg

When

1,500 m to 10 km

AWorks

Beta-alanine

Helps muscles handle fatigue better on 1 to 10 minute efforts. Tingling possible if you take a big dose at once.

Dose

4-6 g/day ×4-12 wk

When

800 m to 5 km

AWorks

Beetroot juice

Improves running economy (+1-3%) in amateur runners. The effect fades in highly trained athletes. No antiseptic mouthwash on race day: it kills the bacteria that activate the beetroot.

Dose

5-15 mmol nitrates

When

2-3 h before

BDepends

Collagen + vitamin C

Doubles tendon collagen production. Useful in case of chronic tendinitis or sessions with jumps/plyometrics.

Dose

15 g + 50 mg

When

30-60 min before session

BDepends

Tart cherry

Reduces muscle soreness and inflammation. Useful after a marathon or ultra. Don't take year-round (could blunt training progress).

Dose

30 ml × 2/day

When

5-7 d before + after race

BDepends

Turmeric

Natural anti-inflammatory. To be absorbed, you need a special form (with black pepper or phytosome). Not for continuous use.

Dose

200-1500 mg/day

When

Around the race

BDepends

Probiotics

Reduces colds and gut issues in marathon/ultra. Mix of Lactobacillus + Bifidobacterium bacteria.

Dose

10-30 billion bacteria/day

When

4 wks before race

BDepends

Omega-3

Natural anti-inflammatory. Reduces injuries and speeds recovery. If you eat oily fish twice a week, you can skip it.

Dose

2 g/day

When

Year-round

BDepends

Vitamin D

1 in 2 athletes is deficient in winter in northern Europe. Get a blood test. Target: 30 ng/mL minimum, ideally 40-50.

Dose

2000-4000 IU

When

Winter

BDepends

Iron

Female runners are at risk (1 in 3 lacks iron). Never supplement without a blood test. Take in the morning with vitamin C, away from coffee and tea.

Dose

60-120 mg ×3/wk

When

If ferritin < 35

CDepends

Magnesium

Bisglycinate form (better absorbed, gentle on stomach). Helps sleep and recovery. Useless against cramps (Cochrane 2020 study).

Dose

200-400 mg

Class A: multiple solid proofs. B: decent proofs but in specific cases. C: limited proofs, case by case. D: little or no proof.

Cramps: the real cause (it's not water)

For a century, we believed cramps came from dehydration and lack of minerals. That's wrong. Modern studies have shown the cause is nervous: your muscles get tired, the system controlling them gets disrupted, and the cramp hits. The most striking proof: a sip of pickle juice stops a cramp in under 90 seconds — way too fast to change your blood composition. It's a nerve reflex triggered by the sour taste in the mouth.

Old theory

Lack of water and minerals

Never proven scientifically. Magnesium has no effect on cramps (Cochrane 2020 study).

Current theory

Nerve and muscle fatigue

Late in an effort, the system regulating your muscles gets thrown off. Cramps strike when you push beyond your training level, not when you're dehydrated.

What works

Stretching + pickle juice

Stretching the cramping muscle calms it almost every time. A sip of pickle juice (or mustard) stops the cramp in under a minute. Real prevention: don't start too fast and build your training properly.

Heat: adapt to run better in summer

Adapting to heat is probably the most underused way to run better. In 10 to 14 days, you can gain 5 to 10% blood volume, sweat more efficiently and lose less salt. Bonus: it also improves performance in cool weather. Sauna or hot bath after training are the simplest methods.

12-15 sessions

Sauna after training

30 min at about 87°C right after training, over 3 weeks. Studies: +7% blood volume, +1.9% on 5 km.

6 days in a row

Hot bath

40°C for 40 minutes after training. Comparable effects to sauna. More accessible.

30 min before

Crushed ice before race

Eat 7 to 14 g of crushed ice per kilo of weight. Drops core temperature by 0.3 to 0.5°C. Lets you hold on 19% longer in heat.

2-4 wk camp

Altitude

Sleep high, train low, around 2200-2500 m. Before: get a ferritin blood test. If under 50 ng/mL, the altitude camp is wasted.

Female runners: what's different

Standard recommendations often come from male studies. For women, 4 points deserve special attention: iron (1 in 3 lacks it), protein based on cycle, calcium and vitamin D for bone health, and chronic energy deficit risk (8 in 10 elite women have at least one symptom).

Iron and ferritin

Get iron tested once a year. Target: ferritin above 50 ng/mL (not 30, as often read). If deficient: 60-100 mg of iron every other day, in the morning, with vitamin C, no coffee or tea nearby.

Protein in the second half of the cycle

Increase by 0.1 to 0.2 g/kg in the 2 weeks before your period. Prefer meat, eggs, fish (rich in lysine). No intermittent fasting in this phase.

Calcium and vitamin D

1300-1500 mg of calcium per day if menstrual issues. 800-2000 IU of vitamin D. Critical for bone health: stress fractures are 4.5 times more frequent when periods stop.

Chronic energy deficit — warning signs

If you eat less than 30 calories per kilo of lean mass per day, you enter a risk zone. Signals: periods stopping, chronic fatigue, repeat injuries, low immunity, poor sleep. See a doctor.

10 false beliefs science has dismantled

Fitness marketing spreads ideas that recent studies have torn down. Here are the most stubborn ones, with what science actually says today.

False belief

« You absolutely must eat in the 30 minutes after exercise »

▾

What science says

The real window is 4 to 6 hours to refill energy stores, and 24 to 48 hours for muscle repair. The next meal is enough 9 times out of 10.

Aragon & Schoenfeld 2013, Margolis 2021 studies

False belief

« The 4 sugars to 1 protein mix is ideal for recovery »

▾

What science says

Protein doesn't help refill energy stores if you already eat enough sugar. The apparent effect just comes from the added calories.

Synthesis of 19 studies (Margolis 2021)

False belief

« Magnesium prevents cramps »

▾

What science says

No proven effect on cramps in athletes. Placebo. Cramps come from nervous fatigue, not mineral deficiency.

Cochrane 2020 study, Schwellnus' work

False belief

« Coffee dehydrates »

▾

What science says

False for those who drink it regularly. Major study: 4 cups a day hydrate as much as water. Coffee counts in your daily fluid total.

Killer 2014 study (PLOS One)

False belief

« If you're thirsty, you're already dehydrated »

▾

What science says

Thirst kicks in exactly when your performance starts to drop (1-2% dehydration). It's a reliable signal you should listen to.

International hydration consensus 2015

False belief

« Creatine bulks you up and hurts runners »

▾

What science says

The +0.5 to 1.5 kg is water in muscles, not fat. Very useful for ultras, trail, seniors and double-session periods.

Forbes 2023, Davies 2024 studies

False belief

« BCAAs help recovery »

▾

What science says

Useless if you eat enough protein. A Greek yogurt or chicken serving has as many BCAAs as a supplement, with the other amino acids you also need.

ISSN 2024 official position

False belief

« For a marathon, 3 days of starvation then 3 days of loading »

▾

What science says

Method outdated since 2002. Today: 36 to 48 hours at 10-12 g of carbs per kilo, no starvation phase. More effective, much less grueling.

Bussau 2002, Burke 2019 studies

False belief

« The more you drink, the better »

▾

What science says

False and dangerous. Drinking too much dilutes blood sodium and can kill (Cynthia Lucero, Boston Marathon 2002). Drink to thirst. Max around 800 ml per hour.

NEJM 2005 study, Hew-Butler 2017

False belief

« High-dose antioxidants speed recovery »

▾

What science says

Vitamin C and E at high dose, taken daily, BLOCK training progress. Free radicals produced by exercise are signals that trigger your adaptation.

Paulsen 2014 study (J Physiol)
